qs.q: According to the American College of Rheumatology criteria, what percentage of sensitivity and specificity is achieved when a patient meets 4 of the 11 criteria?
qs.e: The presence of 4 of the 11 ACR criteria yields a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 95% for SLE. This established threshold aids clinicians in diagnosing and subclassifying the disease.

qs.q: Which diagnostic modality yields the highest sensitivity and specificity for detecting Trichomonas vaginalis?
qs.e: Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests such as the Aptima assay are considered the most sensitive and specific diagnostic tests, boasting sensitivities around 97%. Wet mount microscopy, by contrast, has a significantly lower sensitivity of about 60%.

qs.q: What percentage of the 1987 or 1997 ACR criteria must be met to achieve an 88% sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing SLE?
qs.e: Meeting at least 4 out of the 11 ACR criteria yields an 88% sensitivity and specificity for SLE. Meeting fewer than 4 criteria lacks this established diagnostic reliability.

qs.q: A medical officer suspects viral encephalitis in a patient presenting with acute fever and altered mental status. Which diagnostic modality offers the highest sensitivity and specificity for detecting viral nucleic acid directly from cerebrospinal fluid?
o: Viral cell culture with cytopathic effect
qs.e: Molecular PCR tests detect viral nucleic acid directly and are the gold standard for diagnosing viral infections in CSF due to their high sensitivity and specificity. Serology and culture are generally slower or used for past exposure or isolation.
qs.s: Medical Virology Semester 3 Crash Revision: MCQs

qs.q: A patient is admitted with severe chest pain that started 4 hours ago. Several cardiac biomarkers are ordered to assess for myocardial infarction. Which of the following markers is the gold standard due to its highest sensitivity and specificity for cardiac injury?
o: Cardiac troponin I or T from myocardium
Total serum creatine kinase from muscle
qs.e: Troponin I or T is the gold standard cardiac biomarker because it is the most sensitive and specific for myocardial necrosis. Myoglobin rises earlier than troponin, but it lacks cardiac specificity as it is also found in skeletal muscle.

ai.subject: Public health
ai.summary: Sensitivity and specificity measure how well a test identifies disease and non‑disease. High sensitivity rules out disease; high specificity rules in disease. They guide screening and diagnostic decisions worldwide.

sections.p: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive; specificity is the proportion without the disease who test negative. They are intrinsic test properties, independent of disease prevalence.
Sensitivity and specificity themselves are not staged, but they affect how we interpret test results across disease stages. Early disease often has lower sensitivity, later stages higher.
Poor sensitivity may stem from low pathogen load, early disease, or suboptimal specimen collection. Low specificity often results from cross‑reactivity, similar antigens, or technical errors.
b: Early infection or low parasite density
Cross‑reactive antibodies (e.g., malaria vs. other febrile illnesses)

sections.p: Clinicians see discordant results: a positive test in a healthy person (false positive) or a negative test in a sick person (false negative). Recognising patterns helps avoid misdiagnosis.
Choose tests based on the clinical question and resource availability. When a gold‑standard test is unavailable, combine imperfect tests to improve overall accuracy.

t.b: Does the patient currently have malaria? High sensitivity needed for screening; if unavailable, use thick smear microscopy.
Has the patient been exposed to HIV? High specificity reduces false positives; confirm positives with Western blot or PCR if possible.
Is there myocardial injury? Very high sensitivity for early MI; specificity helps differentiate from other causes of chest pain.

sections.p: Relying on a test with low sensitivity in a high‑risk patient may miss life‑threatening disease; low specificity may lead to unnecessary treatment and toxicity.
b: False‑negative sepsis screen in immunocompromised patients
False‑positive TB test leading to unnecessary therapy

sections.p: Treat based on clinical suspicion, not solely on test results. Use high‑sensitivity tests to rule out disease, then confirm with high‑specificity tests before starting definitive therapy.
b: If rapid malaria test negative but suspicion high, treat empirically and obtain thick smear.
Positive HIV ELISA → confirm before starting antiretrovirals.

sections.p: Repeat testing when disease prevalence changes or after treatment to assess cure. Educate patients on test limitations to avoid false reassurance.
b: Post‑treatment TB sputum culture to confirm clearance.
Annual HIV screening in high‑risk groups.

sections.p: Sensitivity/specificity are sometimes mixed up with predictive values, which depend on disease prevalence.
b: Positive predictive value = probability disease is present when test is positive.
Negative predictive value = probability disease is absent when test is negative.

sections.p: In low‑prevalence settings, even a test with high specificity can yield many false positives; in high‑prevalence settings, a test with modest sensitivity can miss cases.
b: Screening mammography in young women → many false positives.
Rapid COVID‑19 antigen test in asymptomatic carriers → false negatives.

faq.q: Why can a test be highly specific but not very sensitive?
faq.a: It detects only true disease cases (few false positives) but may miss many because the marker is absent in early or mild disease.

faq.q: How does disease prevalence affect predictive values?
faq.a: Higher prevalence raises the positive predictive value and lowers the negative predictive value, even if sensitivity and specificity stay constant.

faq.q: What should I do if the best test is unavailable?
faq.a: Combine a high‑sensitivity screening test with clinical assessment, and if needed, use an alternative test with known performance characteristics.

exam: Explain the difference between sensitivity and specificity and give a clinical scenario where each is most important.
A rapid malaria test has 95% sensitivity and 85% specificity. In a region with 10% prevalence, calculate the positive predictive value.
Describe how you would manage a patient with a negative HIV ELISA but high clinical suspicion of infection.
